1 | Hydrocarbon Core Scanning (HCS™) of 7 | wells from the Sleipner field | Summary. | Slabbed cores from 7 wells in the Sleipner field has been scanned for residual | hydrocarbon contents and type. In Well 15/9-1 only the interval 3648-3667 m | contain distinct shows, of heavy oil. The oil column of well 15/9-B-4T2 appears to | be divided into several segments, containing variable amounts of oils with | contrasting density and composition. The segments are commonly separated by | dry sections (barriers?), that may cause compartmentalization. Only the top | section (2648-2660.5 m) of well 15/9-9 displays distinct and continuous oil shows | (heavy and medium oil), while the lower sections show occasional short segments | with shows down to 2750 m. The section below this depth is dry. The whole core | interval of well 15/9-13 is dry. All data points with high fluorescence intensity in this | well (up to 5000 counts) are coming from carbonates. 3 | 2.3 Mineral fluorescence and fluorescing contaminants | In addition to measurements from hydrocarbons, the logs may include data from | interfering fluorescing mineral cements (i.e. carbonates) or contamination of drilling | muds. | Carbonate versus petroleum  fluorescence: | Minerals do normally not show fluorescence. The lower software threshold of 800 | counts automatically exclude post-processing of measurements due to the low | mineral background fluorescence. The only significant exception is carbonates, | which may occur as both non-fluorescent and fluorescent  types. If the carbonates | fluoresce, the fluorescence is always within the | visible | part of the spectrum. | Fluorescence behaviour of hydrocarbons may, in contrast, be invisible to a human | eye. Hydrocarbon condensates commonly fluoresce in the invisible ultraviolet (UV) | part of the spectrum,  whereas asphaltenes fluoresce in the invisible near-infrared | (NIR) part of the spectrum.
